name: Hedged Requests and Tail Latency
intent: Cut the slowest requests at scale: send a duplicate to a second replica when the first is slow, and take whichever answers first.
scenario: A search request queries 50 shards in parallel and waits for all of them. Each shard answers in about 10 ms, but 1% of calls take 200 ms to a second. About 40% of searches now include one slow shard, so the user-visible p99 is the shards' rare worst case, not their typical case.
problem: Averages hide the tail, and fan-out multiplies it. If one backend is slow 1% of the time and a user request waits for N of them, the chance that at least one is slow is 1 - 0.99^N: 9.6% for 10, 39.5% for 50, 63.4% for 100. Each cause is ordinary (a GC pause, a compaction, a noisy neighbour, a cold cache, a deep queue, a retry), cannot be fixed everywhere, and a timeout does not help because the request is slow, not failed. The latency users feel is the maximum over many calls, so it is set by the rarest delays.

howItWorks.title: Measure the tail per backend and per user request
howItWorks.text: Record p50, p95, p99 and p99.9 of each backend call and of the whole fan-out request. Averages and p50 look healthy while the user request is dominated by the slowest of N calls. The per-backend p99 is the number that gets amplified.

howItWorks.title: Send a backup request after a delay
howItWorks.text: Send the call to one replica. If it has not answered within a hedge delay, typically the backend's p95, send the same call to a second replica and use whichever answer arrives first, then cancel the loser. Only about 5% of calls ever get a second copy, but those are exactly the calls that were headed for the tail. Dean and Barroso (The Tail at Scale) report a Bigtable read benchmark where hedging after 10 ms cut the 99.9th percentile by about 96% for around 2% more requests.

howItWorks.title: Tie requests to cancel cheaply
howItWorks.text: A tied request goes to two replicas at once, each carrying the identity of the other. When one starts executing it tells the other to drop the request. The duplicate costs a queue slot but almost no CPU, and it removes the hedge delay for the wait-in-queue part of the tail. It needs a cancel path that is faster than the work and replicas that can see each other.

howItWorks.title: Make the delay adaptive and budget the extra load
howItWorks.text: Keep a rolling latency histogram per backend and set the delay to its current p95 (or p90 to p99), so the delay rises when the backend is genuinely slower. Cap hedges at a fraction of traffic (a token bucket refilled at 5% of calls) and drop hedges when the backends are overloaded. A fixed 13 ms delay that was right yesterday becomes a load amplifier when latencies drift.

howItWorks.title: Hedge only what is safe, and shorten the tail at the source
howItWorks.text: A hedged request executes twice, so hedge reads or idempotent operations, or make the write idempotent with a key. Then attack the causes: break work into small units, spread hot data over micro-partitions, replicate hot items selectively, send canary requests to one or two servers before the full fan-out, remove GC and background-job stalls, and shed load before queues build.

pros: Attacks the actual cause of a bad p99 at scale: the maximum over many calls
Cheap when tuned: a p95 delay hedges about 5% of calls (the Bigtable benchmark above needed roughly 2% extra requests) and the tail can shrink by an order of magnitude
Works against transient, uncorrelated slowness (GC, noisy neighbour, a busy queue) that you cannot remove everywhere
Needs no knowledge of why a replica was slow
cons: Adds load, and load is what makes tails worse; mistuned hedging is a self-inflicted overload
Requires replicas that can serve the request, and idempotent or read-only operations
Does not help when the slowness is correlated: a bad deploy, a shared database, a saturated network or a hot key slows every replica together
Hides unhealthy replicas: hedging masks a slow node, so latency stays good until the node is bad enough to matter
Needs good per-backend latency metrics and a working cancellation path
whenToUse: Wide fan-out reads (search, feeds, scatter-gather, multi-shard lookups) where p99 of the user request matters
Read paths with several replicas of the same data and latency that is variable but not saturated
Systems that already track latency percentiles per backend and have spare capacity (10 to 30%)
whenNotToUse: Backends that are already near saturation: the extra requests make everything slower
Non-idempotent writes, or any call with side effects you cannot deduplicate
Fan-out of 1 or 2 where the p99 of a single backend is already acceptable and a timeout plus retry is enough
When the slowness is the whole service (an overloaded dependency): use load shedding, backpressure and a circuit breaker instead
pitfalls: Hedging after the p50: about half of all calls are duplicated, utilisation jumps and the cluster tips over (the simulation shows 100% extra load)
A static delay that was measured once: when load rises the normal latency passes the delay, almost everything hedges, and the extra load keeps the latency high
Not cancelling the loser, so slow requests keep consuming CPU on the replica that was already slow
Hedging non-idempotent operations such as a payment or an order, which then happens twice
Using the same connection, thread pool or replica for both copies, so the hedge shares the cause of the slowness
Mixing this up with retries: a retry waits for a failure and backs off, a hedge fires while the first call is still in flight and does not wait

roles.label: Search service
roles.description: Fans a user request out to the shards and waits for all of them.

roles.label: Shard replica
roles.description: One copy of a data partition that answers part of the query; usually fast, occasionally slow.

roles.label: Hedge logic
roles.description: Tracks the latency percentile, fires the backup after the delay, takes the first answer and cancels the other.

quiz.question: A search request fans out to 100 backends in parallel and waits for all of them. Each backend independently takes much longer than usual on 1% of calls. Roughly what share of user searches contains at least one slow call?
options: Roughly 1% of searches, because each backend is slow so rarely
Roughly 10% of searches, because the rare delays add up linearly
Roughly 63% of searches, since the chance of no slow call is about 37%
Roughly 99% of searches, because with this many calls a delay is certain
quiz.explanation: The chance that none of 100 calls is slow is 0.99 to the power 100, about 37%, so about 63% of requests hit a slow one. The user sees the slowest of all calls, so rare per-backend delays become common.

quiz.question: A read goes to one of three replicas. The backend latency is p50 8 ms, p95 30 ms, p99 200 ms. You want to cut the tail while adding only about 5% extra load. When should a backup request go to a second replica?
options: Immediately to two replicas on every call, then take whichever answer arrives first
After about 30 ms with no reply, then take the first answer
After about 8 ms, so most slow calls get a backup very early
After about 200 ms, since only outliers need help
quiz.explanation: A hedge delay near p95 duplicates only about 5% of calls, the ones heading for the tail. Hedging at p50 would duplicate about half the traffic, and waiting for p99 leaves most of the tail untouched.

quiz.question: A bad deploy makes every replica of a service five times slower. Reads use hedging with a fixed 30 ms delay that was the p95 last week. Latency gets worse, not better. What is the best protection against this?
options: Cap hedges at a small share of calls and let the delay follow the current p95
Send each hedge to three replicas instead of two, so at least one is likely to be fast
Lower the fixed delay so hedges fire sooner and rescue calls before they get slow
Add a client timeout of 100 ms with an immediate retry on the same replica set
quiz.explanation: The slowness is shared by all replicas, so nearly every call passes the fixed delay and the extra copies double the load. A hedge budget and an adaptive delay stop hedging from amplifying an overload, while the other options add even more load.
